PCI.BIO:
Dr. Srivastava received his doctoral degree in Mechanical Engineering from Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur, India in 1985. In 1996, he moved to Cincinnati, OH, USA and joined TechSolve, Inc. He served TechSolve Inc. for eighteen (18) years in various capacities, finally as Chief Technology Officer. He received more than fourteen million ($18,000,000) dollar research grant from NIST, DoD, AFRL and NSF. Dr. Srivastava has been member of several International Technical Organizations such as ASM International, SME, ASME, and CIRP. He has served on the Board of SME/NAMRI as Director during 2010-2013. He has been an invited/keynote speaker internationally and an editorial board member for the Journal of Manufacturing Technology Research and the International Journal of Nanomanufacturing. He has presented his work in USA, Canada, Germany, Italy, France, Brazil, India and China. He is the Fellow SME 2020 and Fellow ASME 2020.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The goal of this project is to develop and sustain the DOE Consortium of Advanced Additive Manufacturing Research and Education for Energy Related Systems (DOE CA2REERs) to expose, recruit, engage and train students from underrepresented groups for a career in Advanced Manufacturing for Energy, following a collaborative approach by a team of investigators from 3 MSI institutions and 2 DOE Labs. The minority serving education institutions include: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (90% Hispanic), University Texas San Antonio (54% Hispanic), and University of Arizona (30% minority). The DOE/NNSA labs are Oak Ridge National Lab and Los Alamos National Lab. The consortium covers minority communities at three minority serving institutions with a total student enrollment of around 100,000 (UTRGV 27,708, UTSA 32,101, and University of Arizona 44,831). The long-term vision of the consortium is to cultivate an innovation driven manufacturing education ecosystem for Energy Innovation with programs designed to recruit young talents and prepare them with solid education and real-life experiences in energy innovation and advanced manufacturing technologies. Upon graduation, students are ready for a dream career in DOE/NNSA labs and energy industries.

Standards/Guidance for Rapid Qualification of Metal-Based Additive Manufacturing
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) is partnering with leading institutions from the DOD-sponsored I-DREAM4D consortium for advanced additive manufacturing and smart manufacturing (University of Texas – Rio Grande Valley [UTRGV], University of Texas – Austin [UTexas], and Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University [VT]) and with the Applied Research Laboratory at Penn State University (ARL PSU) to propose this project for developing Standards/Guidance for Rapid Qualification of Metal-based Additive Manufacturing (AM). The work is focused on equipping the many Technical Authorities, who must ultimately evaluate and approve AM processes and parts for use within various industry segments, to apply best practice qualification methods/tools that can be suitably validated. The term “rapid qualification” indicates our focus on integrating model-based approaches for conducting verification and validation (V&V) activities on AM parts/processes and expert system guidance with reduced traditional physical testing so that Technical Authority qualification can keep up with the growing expansion in the use of AM across many industries. Without development and validation of such standards/guidance, Technical Authority qualification may become a critical path roadblock that will slow the adoption and expansion of AM applications.
The proposed approach leverages unique institutional and personnel capabilities of our co-investigating partners to do the following: (1) Develop a recommended standard/guide for Technical Authorities for implementing best practices in rapid qualification of AM applications, (2) Develop an expert system of recommended guidance on the best uses of AM technologies for different types of applications and associated V&V activities that should be considered for these applications, (3) Develop standard approaches for evaluating and accepting model-based approaches for supporting V&V of AM applications, (4) Develop new best practice model-based approaches for supporting V&V of AM applications, (5) Demonstrate the use of the new standards/guidance for actual AM applications, including demonstration of the standard approach for evaluating and accepting model-based approaches, and (6) Document the recommended standards/guidance in a publication that any Technical Authority may use in setting their own requirements within their industry. Table 1 summarizes how this proposed project addresses the evaluation criteria for this Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO).

CONGRANT.TITLE: Directed Energy Deposition Hybrid Manufacturing Technology for Research and Education in Advanced Materials for the Defense
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This request is made on behalf of the DoD Consortium for Innovation Driven Research Education for Advanced Manufacturing for the Defense (I-DREAM4D, www.idream4d.org) funded by DoD through the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering (Award number N00014-19-1-2728), with a total amount of $3,958,812. The consortium is composed of five higher education institution members (UTRGV, UT Austin, UTSA, Virginia Tech, Virginia State University), one national research center, two national labs (Army Research Lab, Oak Ridge National Lab), members from defense industry (Honeywell, Huntington Ingalls Industries, Raytheon, Northrop Grumman, Boeing Global Services & Support, and StandardAero), local high schools, and community colleges. The requested Directed Energy Deposition (DED)Hybrid Manufacturing Technology facilitates the goal of the consortium, which is to advance research in material engineering through additive manufacturing (AM) and smart manufacturing (SM) technologies and to support defense innovations for lightweight materials, structures and systems at extreme conditions. This requested technology is crucial for the long-term vision of the consortium to sustain an innovation driven manufacturing research and education ecosystem to educate future scientists and engineers who lead U.S. defense manufacturing innovation.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Intelligent Monitoring and Control of Grinding Process
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
surface integrity is a dynamic, complex, and nonlinear process. This complexity causes considerable
difficulty in optimally designing a monitoring and control system consisting of sensors that collect the
data, and mechanisms that build and update models from this data; and also use these models to control
the process in real-time. The specific process targeted by PI's research is of the grinding systems from the
manufacturing/production domain. A precise and deep understanding of the interaction among (i) the
sensor system, (ii) the physical process of grinding, and (iii) the parameters controlling the grinding
operation, plays an important role in the overall performance of the underlying grinding system. In order
to capture this precise and deep understanding of the process dynamics, we need the capability to
transform the data generated by the sensor system into succinct models that provide the following critical
pieces of information: (i) parameters for monitoring the process; and (ii) all inferences and parameters
needed for effective and efficient control of the process. The main focus of the research proposed here is
on the following tasks: (a) Derivation of models of interest from vast data streams; (b) Use of these
derived models for process control; and (c) Methodologies for dynamically selecting suitable models and
also updating some of the model parameters in response to sensed process data in real-time. These
capabilities will be developed and validated in a test-bed environment consisting of grinding machines
supported by an elaborate infrastructure consisting of sensors, electro-mechanical control mechanism and
monitoring and data recording support.

Advanced Robotics Academy for Rio Grande Valley, Texas
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Manufacturing, in general, has a perception of old, smoky work places with repetitive jobs, lack of technology and no advancement prospects. However, the latest studies and reports from professional organizations and national advisory boards agree that the American Manufacturing industry is in significant need of talents with necessary skills for innovation, cultural understanding, and the understanding multidisciplinary advanced manufacturing technologies. Robots are being increasingly used across industry sectors to improve productivity through automation while maintaining product quality. Workers need up-to-date knowledge and skills to maintain and use existing robots. To have a workforce of such skilled workers, there is a significant need for industrial certification programs in robotics. It is critical that education efforts respond to the demand for robotics specialists by offering courses and professional certification in robotics and automation. The goal of this proposed project is to create and sustain a strong collaborative effort to develop a “Regional Advanced Robotics Academy (RARA)” in Rio Grande Valley, a region of South Texas.

CONGRANT.TITLE: INNOVATIVE CUTTING TOOL TECHNOLOGY FOR HIGH SPEED MACHINING OF
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
This research project is proposing an innovative approach in order to advance the
state-of-the-art in design and development of cutting tool to enhance machinability of high
strength aerospace alloys thus supporting the competitiveness of the commercial and military
aerospace industry in the U.S. These industries impose high demands on production systems
due to the high cost of aerospace materials, poor machinability of such materials and strict
product safety requirements. As a result of increased need for quality and low cost, there is a
great need for developing cutting tools with required properties such as sustaining hardness at
high temperatures and higher thermal conductivity. While designing and developing such cutting
tools, modeling techniques are required to select optimum cutting tool geometry and machining
conditions, improving the machinability of work materials, and reducing the costly experimental
trial and error efforts.
This research work will be conducted with close interaction and technical support from ARL. Dr.
Srivastava (PI) will subcontract the work for designing and developing the cutting tool and then
conduct all cutting tests on the machine tool in the newly developed Manufacturing Innovation
Hub (MIH) at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). PI (Dr. Srivastava) will also
concentrate on physics-based simulation modeling issues related to machining of titanium alloys
(temperatures, shear-localization, cyclical chip formation, and residual stresses). Thus, the
designed experiments and the integration of modeling effort under complex workpiece material
engagement conditions will be conducted at UTRGV. PI will also plan for workshops and
industrial seminars to disseminate the results.

Computational design and additive synthesis of high entropy alloy borides and nano particle additives for discovery of materials and structures with super/ultra-high hardness under extreme thermal and chemical conditions
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The objective of this proposed project is 1) to develop super-hard [1] metal/ceramic compounds (hardness in the range of 40-80 GPa) with multiscale structures and tailored properties in the full 3D space, leveraging a novel high throughput laser additive alloying (LAA) process that 3D forms super-hard high configurational entropy alloy (HEAs) borides compounds directly from multiple principal elements, and 2) to investigate computational methods for quick prediction of materials-processes-properties relationships to efficiently explore and synthesis ultra-hard composites (hardness above 80 GPa) by incorporating ultra-hard nanoparticles such as nano-diamond [2] and boron nitride in the matrix of in-situ formed HEAs.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Advanced Manufacturing
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Titanium and Nickel-based alloys have seen increased utilization in military and aerospace applications because of a combination of high specific strength, toughness, corrosion resistance, elevated-temperature performance and compatibility with polymer composite materials. These material properties are essential requirements for certain critical parts such as wing supports and jet engine components. For decades, the high-speed machining of these alloys has created considerable interest to researchers, tool manufacturers and end users because titanium alloys are difficult to machine due to their inherent low thermal conductivity and higher chemical reactivity with other materials at elevated temperatures. It has been observed that plastic deformation and dissolution wear are two major detrimental mechanisms in high-speed machining of titanium alloys which contribute to tool failure. In addition, thermal cycling due to the serration process at the tool-workpiece interface, affects the tool life significantly.
I plan to conduct research on “High Speed Machining of Titanium Alloys”. The designed experiments will be conducted on a milling machine using different type of coated cutting inserts. The output parameters such as cutting forces, tool-wear/life, surface finish will be measured to compare the performance of various coated tools during the milling operation.  The process optimization will be conducted based on the results.

Innovation Driven Education Pathway for Defense Oriented Advanced Manufacturing Engineering
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The success of the defense industry relies heavily on its innovation capability and its
ability for developing new systems, processes and materials that support innovation needs. While
the challenges facing the defense industry have moved on to a new level in this era, the public
perception of manufacturing remains as not interesting, less rewarding, low tech, dirty and less
secure. This poor perception comes with a lack of interest from young people and a significant gap
of talents needed to drive manufacturing innovation. This proposed project, a joint effort
collaboration of a defense lab, 5 education institutions geographically dispersed across North
America, and 8 defense manufacturers in the U.S. aims to reverse this gap though cultivating an
innovation driven manufacturing education system with instruction covering the total
manufacturing engineering enterprise. The project is designed to attract, engage, train and educate
talent to drive manufacturing and advance manufacturing technologies needed for the future of US
manufacturing and the defense industries.
To accomplish this agenda, a consortium led by the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
(UTRGV) and including, the University of Texas Austin (UT Austin), the University of Texas San
Antonio (UTSA), Virginia State University (Virginia State) and Michigan State University (MSU)
partner with the Army Research Laboratory (ARL) and industry collaborators including the United
Launch Alliance (ULA), Boeing, Ingalls Shipbuilding, Raytheon, StandardAero, Honeywell,
Navistar, and Intrex Aerospace. This geographically distributed team also includes high schools,
typically local to a university, and Career and Technical Education (CTEs) organizations to
provide both secondary and post-secondary activities to generate a pathway system.
Activities that are undertaken to support this pathway include: a research exchange program which
includes student joint supervision with ARL, preparation of Manufacturing Engineers to join and
lead defense industries including development of a defense manufacturing engineering
concentration, a defense and summer research program, a faculty exchange program, a summer
innovation camp for high school students, and student manufacturing exposure programs to assist
with student recruiting. As a result of responding to these multiple goals with corresponding
actions, the consortium team meets the needs of the multiple constituencies that it serves. Students
have a pathway from high school to an assignment in advanced manufacturing for defense
industries, and the industries have a direct opportunity to attract and hire qualified technical talent.
Our proposal focuses on Innovative Advanced Manufacturing and specifically on Systems and
Materials, and Additive Manufacturing Technologies which are capable of producing lightweight
structures and materials. This tightly targeted approach has been encouraged by ARL, our military
laboratory partner, and the defense industry partners in our consortium: Boeing, Raytheon,
Honeywell, Ingalls Shipbuilding, United Launch Alliance, and others.

CONGRANT.TITLE: An Integrated Real Time Smart Manufacturing Technology Based Work System for Productivity Monitoring and Management
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The purpose of this work is to establish a real time productivity monitoring and management system. This system will be based on enhanced productivity measurement and control tools providing an extended work science tool kit. This will lead to smarter work design and measurement, smarter production planning capabilities, improved energy usage and production flexibility among other potential benefits.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Talent Development for Smart Manufacturing
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This proposed effort will 1) develop and offer a summer certificate program for executives, engineers and undergraduate students with a focus on smart manufacturing science and technology; and 2) develop a Master of Science in Manufacturing Engineering with concentration in smart manufacturing and manufacturing analytics. These two programs are proposed recognizing the needs for talents required to drive innovation in smart manufacturing. It aims to prepare students/professionals with multidisciplinary knowledge and research experiences in related fields, which is not readily provided within existing traditional engineering programs. These two talent development programs prepare students with theories and tools in information collection and modeling, sensor, robotics, data mining, data analytics and science, artificial intelligence, systems, and decision models which can be used to monitor, predict, control and improve the behavior and performance of materials, structures, products, processes, services, and systems ranging from micro-scale to macro-scale. Students in MS program will conduct multidisciplinary research related to smart technologies or lead innovation in manufacturing industries.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Two Machine Negotiation Based Smart Coordination and Optimization for Smart Manufacturing System
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The goal of the proposed work is to investigate suitability of negotiation based automated system coordination and optimization in the context of smart manufacturing at strategic, tactical, and operational levels. While the focus of the phase 1 project is at operational level, this work can be reused and scaled up to cover following decision scenarios: 1) at strategic level, smart machines negotiate for longer term system design and layout. 2) at tactical level, smart machines negotiate and decide short term scheduling and work order assignments 3) at operational level, negotiation is utilized to achieve real time smart machine coordination and system optimization.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Enhanced Hybrid Model to Predict the Surface Roughness of Honed Cylinder Bore
Modeling and optimization of process parameters in face-milling of Ti6Al4V alloy using Taguchi and gray relational analysis

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Titanium alloys are extensively used in aerospace, missiles, rockets, naval ships, automotive, medical devices, and even the consumer electronicsindustry where a high strength to density ratio, lightweight, high corrosion resistance, and resistance to high temperatures are important. Themachining of these alloys has always been challenging for manufacturers. This article investigates the combined effect of radial depth, cuttingspeed and feed rate on cutting forces, tool life, and surface roughness during face milling of Ti6Al4V alloy. This study focuses on the significanceof radial depth of cut on cutting force, tool life and surface roughness compared to that of cutting speed and feed rate during face milling ofTi6Al4V alloy. In this paper, mono and multi-objective optimization of the response characteristics have been conducted to find out the optimalinput parameters, namely, cutting speed, feed rate, and radial depth of cut. Taguchi method and analysis of variance (ANOVA) analysis havebeen used for mono-objective optimization, while Taguchi-based grey relational analysis has been used for multi-objective optimization. Theregression analysis has been performed for developing mathematical models to predict the surface roughness, tool life, and cutting forces.According to ANOVA analysis, the most significant parameters for tool life and cutting force (FY) are cutting speed, and radial depth of cut,respectively, while feed rate is observed to be the most significant parameter for surface roughness and force (FX). The optimal combination ofinput parameters for tool life and FY are 50m/min cutting speed, 0.02mm/rev feed rate, and 7.5mm radial depth of cut. However, the optimalparameters for surface roughness are 65m/min cutting speed, 0.02mm/rev feed rate, and 7.5mm radial depth of cut. For FX, the optimal conditionis observed as cutting speed 57.5m/min, 0.02mm/rev feed rate, and 7.5mm radial depth of cut. A validation experiment, conducted at the optimalparameters of surface roughness, shows an improvement of 31.29% compared to the surface roughness at initial condition. Taguchi-based greyrelational analysis for multi-objective optimization shows an improvement of 55.81%, 6.12%, and 23.98% in tool life, surface roughness, andFY, respectively. ANOVA analysis based on grey relational grade shows that the radial depth of cut is the most significant parameter for multiobjectiveoptimization during the face milling of Ti6Al4V.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: A Hybrid Physical Model Based Artificial Neural Network Approach to Predict Surface Roughness in Engine Cylinder Bore Honing
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: This study proposes a hybrid model that utilizes an analytical model and Artificial Neural Networks(ANN) to predict surface roughness in cylinder bore honing. As the heart of internal combustion engine technology any improvement in the tribological properties of cylinder bore can lead to friction reduction, which in turn can enhance engine performance. Serving as the terminal process in the production of cylinder bore, the required surface roughness is imparted by honing. Cylinder bore honing consists of rough, fine and plateau honing and numerous variables like stone geometry, grit size, grain concentration, speed, pressure, feed, over travel, number of strokes. Different approaches are used to determine parameters to predict surface roughness but all of these approaches have their drawback, for experimental based studies are limited by number of parameters that can be considered, analytical models are limited by the computational time, while machine learning approaches require a large amount of data to be trained. To overcome this limitation, this study employs a hybrid model to investigate the evolution of roughness at a rough and fine stage of honing process. A two phase approach is used first a physical model is employed to generate results using various parameters. Afterwards this data is used to train the ANN that can predict surface roughness for new parameters. The developed model can make predictions in one tenth of the time with less than 20% difference from the simulated values.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Application of optimized laser surface re-melting process on selective laser melted 316L stainless steel inclined parts

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Lower surface quality of selective laser melting (SLM) manufactured parts remains to be a key shortcoming particularly for high performance functional components. In this paper, the authors utilized Box–Behnken methodology to explore the effect of laser surface re-melting process parameters. The process parameters are:laser power, laser exposure time, laser point distance, and shell layer thickness. The experiments were conducted using Renishaw AM-250 machine. SLM manufactured parts with inclination of 45˚ up-skin were treated with a given surface roughness using laser surface re-melting (LSR). The optimization of process para-meters was conducted using response surface methodology and the validation tests was carried out utilizing the determined input parameters. The results verified the effectiveness of the integrated approach and the proposed statistical model. The outcomes of this study demonstrated that selective laser melting process followed by the laser surface re-melting process is very likely to become a fast and economic integrated method for improving the inclined surface quality of SLM manufactured parts.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Renewable Energies: Reducing Cost-by-Expansion of The RGV Electric Utility Companies.
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Institute of Industrial and Systems Engineers
INTELLCONT.EDITORS: H.E. Romejin, A. Schafer. R. Thomas
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: According to Interstate Renewable Energy Council (IREC), Renewable energy systems are becoming prevalent and economically accessible for small-town municipalities in South Texas. Nowadays, the two most popular energy sources of the electrical utility companies, in the Rio Grande Valley (RGV), are coal and natural gas. When these companies think about an expansion in the electrical capacity, they face major economic issues escalated by the high costs of the current energy sources. The intention is to reduce cost by expansion of RGV electrical utility companies by knowing what fraction of their electrical current sources, a renewable energy system can provide while being economically advantageous unlike only a capacity based on coal and natural gas. This research will assess a renewable energy system as the third energy source for these electrical utility companies. The primary aim of this paper is to conduct the concept of levelized cost of energy (LCOE) to evaluate three renewable energy sources and determine which one is the most economically sustainable in RGV. To address the reliability and verify the results, a sensitivity analysis is conducted by executing a C++ code of the LCOE parameters of this research. The paper concludes that that depending on the technology employed; wind energy is the least expensive per unit (MWh).

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Optimization and analysis of surface roughness for INVAR-36 in end milling operations
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
INVAR-36 has 36% Ni resulting very low co-efficient of thermal expansion. Low co-efficient of thermal expansion leads Invar-
36 to be used in the applications where dimensional stability is an important criteria. In such critical applications surface
roughness affects significantly to the performance. L9 orthogonal array obtained by Taguchi method was used in this industry
supported research work. Three factors at three levels were chosen and each experiment was replicated four times.Data was
collected using Taylor Hobson (Surtronic S128) roughness tester and analysed by S/N ratio method and ANOVA method which
concluded that axial depth of cut has highest impact on surface roughness which is followed by cutting speed and feed rate
respectively. The results have been shared with the sponsored industry and industry is expected to be benefited in terms of
improving surface roughness values.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Titanium pipes are being used in number of industrial application due to its superior strength to weight ratio, corrosion resistance, fatigue resistance and crack growth. Although Titanium has superior material properties but its machining and finishing is still a very difficult task. In present work, an extended magnetic tool has been used to finish internal surface of titanium (grade 2) pipe (Ø89.5 x Ø79.5 x 305 mm). An extended magnetic tool has been developed from small permanent magnet having its N-S poles made up of Nd-Fe-B permanent magnets (24 x 12 x 25 mm). Response surface methodology has been used to design the experiments. Effect of four major process parameters- processing time, pole-work gap, surface rotational speed and electrolytic iron particle size on percent improvement in surface finish has been analyzed. Microscopic images of processed surfaces also demonstrate the influence of selected process parameters.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Finish Turning of Ti-6Al-4V with the Atomization-Based Cutting Fluid (ACF) Spray System
A New Microstructure-Sensitive Flow Stress Model for the High Speed Machining of Titanium Alloy Ti-6Al-4V
Finish Turning of Ti-6Al-4V with the Atomization-Based Cutting Fluid (ACF) Spray System
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Product quality and productivity are important factors in manufacturing industries, especially when dealing with cumbersome materials like titanium. Cooling and lubrication effects offered by the associated metalworking fluid application system play a vital role in determining these factors, especially during finish cutting. Recently, the atomization-based cutting fluid (ACF) spray system has shown promising cooling and lubrication effects during rough turning of titanium at the macro-scale, but yet to be examined during finish cutting (e.g., depth of cut and feed rate 0.2. mm or lower). This paper aims to study the effect of the ACF spray system on machining performance during finish turning of Ti-6Al-4V. In the first set of experiments, two spray parameters (viz., gas velocity and flow rate) and cutting parameters (viz., cutting speed, feed rate and depth of cut) are varied to select the most suitable condition for the application of the ACF spray system. Machining outputs are evaluated in terms of nose wear, cutting temperature, surface roughness, roundness error, chip morphology, and part hardness. A separate set of experiments is then performed to compare the performance of the ACF spray system against compressed air (dry) and flood coolant conditions. It is found that, even a lower fluid flow rate of 1.5. mL/min (10. vol.%) at a lower gas velocity of the spray system outperforms the other two coolant conditions, thus further enhancing the performance of environmentally-friendly manufacturing process.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Role of phase transformation in chip segmentation during high speed machining of dual phase titanium alloys
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Elsevier - Journal of Materials Processing Technology
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Chip segmentation during machining of titanium alloys is primarily due to adiabatic shear localization associated with thermally driven alpha-beta phase transformation at extremely high speeds. Current constitutive material models used in simulating the machining process ignore the role of phase transformation in shear localization and its influence on the material associated dynamic response. This research presents a new phase approach to chip segmentation that includes a recently developed constitutive material model based on the self-consistent method (SCM) that accounts for material composition, as well as alpha-beta phase transformation, during machining. This SCM-based model is implemented in the finite element framework to validate and predict the effects of starting material property, cutting speeds, uncut chip thicknesses, rake angles, tool radius, and friction coefficients on the strains, temperatures and beta volume fractions in chip segmentation. It confirms that cutting speed and uncut chip thickness have great impact, rake angle has less effect, tool radius and friction coefficient have the least effects on chip segmentation. However, tool geometry as well as machining parameters have great influence on the machined surface in terms of temperature magnitude, affected depth and the associated alpha-beta phase transformation. INTELLCONT.TITLE: Design and evaluation of an atomized-based cutting fluid spray system in turning of titanium alloy
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Tool life has been a vital issue in machining titanium alloys. Recently, an atomization-based cutting fluid
(ACF) application has been found to be an effective approach for cooling and lubrication in micromachining
operations. In this study, an ACF spray system is developed for macro-scale turning of Ti–6Al–4V.
The spray system is designed to minimize interaction between the fluid droplets, and the gas nozzle to
control the divergence of the fluid droplets. Experiments are conducted to study the effect of five specific
ACF spray parameters including fluid flow rate, spray distance, impingement angle, and type and pressure
level of the droplet carrier gas on cutting forces, tool life, and chip characteristics. It has been observed
that the combination of lower pressure (150 psi) air-mixed CO2 with a higher flow rate (20 ml/min) and a
larger spray distance (35 mm) produces a significantly longer tool life and broken chips. The results also
reveal that the ACF spray system can extend tool life up to 40–50% over flood cooling.

Modeling and interpretation of fiber orientation-based failure mechanisms in machining of carbon fiber reinforced polymer composites
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The development and implementation of a microstructure-based finite element model for the machining of carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composites is presented. A new approach to interfacial modeling is introduced where the material interface is modeled using continuum elements, allowing failure to take place in either tension or compression. The model is capable of describing the fiber failure mode occurring throughout the chip formation process. Characteristic fiber length in the chips, and machining forces for microstructures with fibers orientated at 0°, 45°, 90°, and 135° are examined. For model validation purposes, the model-based machining performance predictions are compared to the machining responses from a set of orthogonal machining experiments. A parametric study is presented that identifies a robust tool geometry, which minimizes the effects of fiber orientation and size on the machining forces.

PRESENT.TITLE: Development and Characterization of Cold Spray Coatings for Aerospace and Defense Manufacturing
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Cold Spray is a type of thermal metal spraying which uses heated gas/air to propel metal powder onto the surface of a substrate to create a coating or repair damaged or corroded metal components. The powder feedstock materials are spherical gas atomized metal powders ranging in size from 20-50 microns in diameter for best results. Cold spray systems use low temperatures ranging from 200-900 °C compared to existing additive manufacturing methods which use much higher temperatures to melt metal. These lower heating temperatures only semi-melt the metal powder particles allowing for them to undergo plastic deformation as they are deposited onto the surface of the substrate. The main objective of this project is to develop and characterize cold spray coatings using aluminum, copper, and nickel powders deposited on different substrates varying processing parameters. As cold spray can be used in different coating applications with a wide range of different metals and alloys, coatings have an unlimited range in applications where rapid repair and high-quality coatings are needed. The ease of use of this technology has a promising future in aerospace and defense applications as it provides a low-cost solution in corrosion prevention and repair of damaged components.
